open-question.question: What does one entry under the new `## Noted contradictions` section of `requirements.md` hold: only the two `###` headings of the conflicting `## Decisions` entries, or those headings plus a one-sentence statement of what each entry says and why both cannot hold, given that the next review pass must turn the entry into a self-standing open question and `/derive-tasks` must read from it which pair is known?
open-question.alternative: Each note entry holds only the two `###` headings under `## Decisions` that the conflicting entries sit under, with no quoted text, no statement of what either entry says, and no reason why both cannot hold; the next review pass rereads both entries from `## Decisions` and composes the open question itself, and `/derive-tasks` takes the pair from the two headings. The smallest and least judged record: the answer skill's analyse step writes two names it already holds, nothing in the note can drift from or misparaphrase the entries it points at, and every reason the review needs stays in the entries themselves, where the review's own step-4 rules already have it state what each says. A heading does not always identify an entry: when both conflicting entries sit under one shared heading, or one sits among several `- **Lead.** text` bullets of a topical subsection, two headings name no pair (review step 4 already has to quote enough to tell such entries apart), and the review must re-find the conflict the answer skill already saw, possibly judging no conflict at all; how much that rediscovery matters depends on whether the review re-tests each note or authors it as noted, which a sibling question settles.

Each note entry holds the two `###` headings and, beneath each, the conflicting clause quoted verbatim from that entry (the bold lead and sentence for a bullet entry, the conflicting sentence for a prose paragraph), with no paraphrase and no statement of why both cannot hold. Locates the exact pair even when both entries share one heading or sit among several bullets, and does so without a paraphrase the answer skill could get wrong, so the review and `/derive-tasks` read the very words that conflict and the note records what was seen rather than a judgment about it. Duplicates entry text into a second section, so the note grows with long prose entries and its quote goes stale if either entry is edited before the review runs; it carries no reason why the two cannot hold, so the review still has to reconstruct the conflict from the quotes, and a quote picked too narrowly can hide the clause that actually clashes.

Each note entry holds the two `###` headings (with enough of each entry's lead or opening words to tell them apart where they share a heading or sit among several bullets) plus one sentence, in the answer skill's own words, stating what each entry says and why both cannot hold. The note is self-standing in the shape the review's step-4 question already takes (name each heading, state briefly what each says), so the next review pass can author the open question from the note with the conflict the answer skill saw spelled out, and `/derive-tasks` can read which pair is known and what the clash is without re-deriving it from `## Decisions`. Adds a paraphrase written in the middle of an answer, which can misstate an entry or overstate a refinement as a conflict, and lengthens every note; the sentence is prose that a reader may take as a recorded decision in its own right, and it duplicates what the review step will restate anyway in the question text.

Each note entry holds the full text of the open question the review pass would author for the pair, in review step 4's shape: it names the `###` heading each entry sits under (quoting enough to tell them apart where they share one), states briefly what each says, and asks which entry stands, so the review pass carries it into a block through `add` as written, with a Short Title of its own choosing. Turning a note into a question becomes a copy rather than a composition, so the question that reaches the alternatives pass is worded by the runner that saw the conflict at the moment it was recorded, and the note is already self-standing for both the review and `/derive-tasks`. Moves question authoring into the answer skills, blurring the boundary that makes `review-milestone-requirements` the sole author of question blocks and the answer side a recorder, and the drafted wording can be stale or mis-scoped by the time the review runs; whether the review copies it or re-tests it is a sibling question's to settle, and if it re-tests, the drafted question buys nothing over a one-sentence statement.

open-question.question: Is the `## Noted contradictions` section created empty with every milestone by the milestone-definition tool, so every `requirements.md` carries five sections and the four-section structure stated in `review-milestone-requirements` and `CLAUDE.md` changes, or created by the first single-question answer skill that writes a note and absent from a milestone that never records a conflict?
open-question.alternative: The milestone-definition tool's fixed template in `core/tools/define_milestone.py` gains an empty `## Noted contradictions` heading, so every milestone defined after this release carries five sections from creation; its docstring, `tests/test_define_output.py`, the four-section "document structure" block of `review-milestone-requirements`, and the milestone file structure in `CLAUDE.md` are restated as five sections. The note-writing step still creates the heading when it is absent, for milestones defined before the release (this milestone included, and in-flight milestones in projects already loading the plugin), since there is no migration. When the review pass deletes the last note it deletes only the entries, leaving the empty heading standing. For every newly defined milestone the note writer only appends under a heading that is always there, and the file's shape is one fixed structure that every reader and the structure statements describe without a condition, so the new section is visible as a standing place to look rather than something a reader must know may appear. It changes a tool, its docstring, and its output test, and edits every restatement of the structure, yet still leaves the note writer a create-if-absent path for older milestones, so two creation paths exist; and every milestone, most of which never record a conflict, carries an empty heading that whole-file readers such as `derive-tasks` and `finish-current-milestone` read past. Where the fallback inserts the heading depends on the position the sibling question on the section's position settles.

The milestone-definition tool and its template stay unchanged at four sections. The first note-writing step that records a conflict in a milestone inserts the `## Noted contradictions` heading together with its note; when the review pass turns the last standing note into an open question and deletes it, it deletes the heading too, so the section exists only while at least one note stands. The structure statements in `review-milestone-requirements` and `CLAUDE.md` keep the four sections and add one optional fifth, present only while a note stands. No tool, template, or test changes, a milestone that never records a conflict is byte-for-byte what it is today, and the heading's mere presence means "unresolved notes stand", so a reader (or a finished milestone's file) shows leftover notes without inspecting the section's body. Both writers take on a structural edit: the note writer must insert a heading at the right place and the review pass, which today states it does not edit `requirements.md`, must remove one in addition to the notes, and a missed removal leaves an empty heading that breaks the presence-means-pending reading. Where the heading is inserted depends on the position the sibling question on the section's position settles.

The milestone-definition tool and its template stay unchanged at four sections. The first note-writing step that records a conflict in a milestone inserts the `## Noted contradictions` heading together with its note; the review pass deletes the notes it turns into open questions and leaves the heading standing, so a milestone that has ever noted a conflict keeps the section, empty or not, and one that never has carries none. The structure statements in `review-milestone-requirements` and `CLAUDE.md` keep the four sections and add one optional fifth, created by the first note. No tool, template, or test changes, and each writer has the smallest rule: the note writer creates the heading only if absent, and the review pass removes only note entries, never touching the heading. The file's shape depends on its history, with three states (absent, present and empty, present with notes), so the empty heading carries no meaning and every structure statement must describe a section that may or may not be there. Where the heading is inserted depends on the position the sibling question on the section's position settles.

open-question.question: Where does `## Noted contradictions` sit in `requirements.md`: directly after `## Decisions` and before `## Out of Scope`, or after `## Out of Scope` as the file's last section, given that the fold tool ends the `## Decisions` section at the next column-0 `## ` heading either way?
open-question.alternative: `## Noted contradictions` sits directly after `## Decisions` and before `## Out of Scope`, so the file's order becomes Goal, Relevant starting state, Decisions, Noted contradictions, Out of Scope; the fold tool's `## Decisions` section then ends at the `## Noted contradictions` heading, and a subsection it creates lands immediately above that heading; the position is stated wherever the file's structure is stated (the definition tool's template if the section is created with the milestone, the review pass's document-structure block, `CLAUDE.md`'s milestone file structure). Each note stands right below the `## Decisions` entries whose `###` headings it names, so a reader of the file (the review pass turning notes into questions, `/derive-tasks` applying its tie-break, a person reading the milestone) meets the known conflicts in the same stretch of text as the entries they concern, and `## Out of Scope` stays the closing section it is today. It splits the long-standing Decisions/Out of Scope adjacency, so every hand writer that today anchors an edit on the `## Out of Scope` heading to reach the end of `## Decisions` (the single-question skills' Edit-based fold) must now anchor on whichever heading follows `## Decisions`, and a hand fold anchored the old way would land a decision under the notes; whether the notes heading is always present to anchor on depends on the section-creation question.

`## Noted contradictions` sits after `## Out of Scope` as the file's last section, so the order becomes Goal, Relevant starting state, Decisions, Out of Scope, Noted contradictions; the four existing sections keep their present order and adjacency, `## Decisions` still ends at `## Out of Scope`, and the position is stated wherever the file's structure is stated. Nothing about the four existing sections moves: every writer and reader that relies on `## Decisions` being followed by `## Out of Scope` keeps working unchanged, the template and structure blocks only gain a trailing section, and a transient section that the review pass empties sits at the tail, out of the way of the milestone's durable content. The notes stand apart from the `## Decisions` entries they name, with `## Out of Scope` in between, so a reader must cross sections to set a note beside its pair; a hand edit that appends an `## Out of Scope` entry must now land it above the notes heading, and if the section is created only when the first note is written, that writer appends at the end of the file, where the file-editing tool has no fixed heading to anchor on, only whatever text happens to close `## Out of Scope`.

`## Noted contradictions` sits after `## Relevant starting state` and directly before `## Decisions`, so the order becomes Goal, Relevant starting state, Noted contradictions, Decisions, Out of Scope; `## Decisions` keeps ending at `## Out of Scope`, so the fold tool's landing point and every hand fold's anchor are unchanged, and the position is stated wherever the file's structure is stated. A reader taking the file top to bottom meets the known conflicts before the entries they concern, so the review pass and `/derive-tasks` are warned which pairs are suspect before reading `## Decisions`, while the Decisions/Out of Scope adjacency that every existing fold relies on stays intact. It places a transient, review-emptied section between the milestone's stable context and its decisions, interrupting the Goal, starting state, Decisions reading flow that `specify-milestone-starting-state` and the readers of the file assume, and a note sits above entries it names, which reads as a preface rather than as a record of what the decisions already hold.

No position is prescribed: `## Noted contradictions` is a column-0 `## ` heading wherever its writer places it, each reader locates it by its heading alone, and the structure statements name the section without placing it; the fold tool still ends `## Decisions` at whatever `## ` heading follows it. No ordering rule has to be written into the template, the review pass's structure block, or `CLAUDE.md`, and no writer can violate one, since every reader and the fold tool already find sections by heading rather than by position. Files drift apart across milestones and even between runs, so a person or a hand Edit cannot rely on where the notes are, and whether the heading after `## Decisions` is `## Out of Scope` or the notes heading varies by runner judgment, exactly where hand folds anchor; it is viable only if the section is created by the first note writer rather than by the definition tool, which has to write it somewhere fixed.

open-question.question: Which runtime file carries the step that writes a noted contradiction: the shared answer core `answer-procedure.md`, whose analyse step already asks whether the answer contradicts a standing entry and which all three single-question skills follow, or the hand-answer procedure that only `answer-open-question` and `answer-open-question-with-alternative` follow, leaving `answer-open-question-with-recommendation` writing no note?
open-question.alternative: The note-writing step lives in the shared answer core `core/shared/answer-procedure.md`, as its own numbered step acting on what the analyse step's fourth question (contradicts or supersedes anything already written) found, landing after the fold and before the block's removal. It applies unconditionally, so all three single-question skills write a note: `answer-open-question` and `answer-open-question-with-alternative` through `hand-answer-procedure.md`, and `answer-open-question-with-recommendation` through `answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md`. Neither composing procedure changes, and the core gains a step but no new input and no branch. Detection and recording sit in one file: the analyse question that already finds the conflict is the step that writes it down, so no single-question path finds a contradiction and then has nowhere to put it. One home for the rule serves all three skills, the composing procedures stay unedited, and a recommendation-derived answer that conflicts with a decision the recommender could see (about 9 of the 38 field pairs) gets noted rather than left to the next review pass's own search. The core stops being a recorder that writes only the decision and the removal, and its step 2 sentence that the analysis "is not itself written into the document" must be qualified. The sweep draws on this file's fold step for content rules and on the first two analyse questions, so the note step has to stand outside step 3, or the sweep's draw needs a carve-out, to keep the sweep forming no contradiction judgment. The single-skill recommendation path then judges contradictions while the sweep recording the same kind of pick does not. Whether the step must also create the `## Noted contradictions` section depends on the section-creation sibling.

The note-writing step lives in `core/shared/hand-answer-procedure.md`, which only `answer-open-question` and `answer-open-question-with-alternative` follow. It runs after that procedure's delegation to the recording core, writing a note when the core's analyse step found a contradiction. The answer core stays unchanged, and `answer-open-question-with-recommendation` writes no note, recording its pick as given, the same way the sweep does. The answer core stays a pass-through recorder with no added write, and the line between recording a pick as given (both recommendation paths, single and swept) and judging a hand answer stays clean. It matches where the hand-answer judgment of undermined picks already lives: the procedure that runs only when a human supplied the answer, which is when a conflict with a standing decision is most likely to be unforeseen. The goal names the single-question answer skills without excluding the recommendation one, and the core's analyse step still asks question four on the recommendation path, so a contradiction found there has no written home and is again left to the runner's discretion, as in the field today. The note step also has to act on a finding the delegated core made, so the hand-answer procedure either repeats the contradiction check itself or relies on the core passing that finding back, which the core currently has no way to do.

The note-writing step lives in `core/shared/answer-procedure.md` beside the analyse step that finds the conflict, but it runs only when the caller asks for it through a new optional input. `hand-answer-procedure.md` sets that input, so `answer-open-question` and `answer-open-question-with-alternative` write notes, and `answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md` leaves it unset, so `answer-open-question-with-recommendation` writes none. Detection and writing stay next to each other in the one file whose step 2 already asks the contradiction question, and a recommendation-derived answer still records its pick as given, consistent with the sweep. Neither composing procedure has to reach back into a finding the core made. The core gains an input that switches a write on or off, so it is no longer a recorder that "gained one input and no branch", and both composing procedures must be edited to pass or omit the input. The recommendation path's found contradictions still go unrecorded, as in the hand-answer-only option.

The note-writing step lives in a new shared file, for example `core/shared/note-contradiction-procedure.md`, which owns how a found conflicting pair is written under `## Noted contradictions`. Both composing procedures, `hand-answer-procedure.md` and `answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md`, reference it after their delegation to the core, so all three single-question skills write a note. The answer core stays unchanged apart from its analyse step's finding being handed to that file. It meets the shared-file rule, since the file has two consumers, and it keeps the answer core free of any write beyond the decision and the removal. That leaves the sweep's draw on the core's fold rules and first two analyse questions untouched by construction, while every single-question path still records what it found. It adds a fourth file to the answer chain, so a runner follows skill, composing procedure, core, and then note procedure. The contradiction is found inside the delegated core but written by a file the composing procedure calls afterwards, so the finding has to cross a delegation boundary the procedures currently have no channel for, which risks the note being skipped when the runner does not carry the core's analysis forward.

open-question.question: When a single-question answer skill records an answer to an ordinary question and finds it contradicts a standing `## Decisions` entry of another question, does it always write a note and leave the old entry as it stands, or does it rewrite the old entry when the answer plainly supersedes it and write a note only when the answer does not plainly settle which entry should hold?
open-question.alternative: Every contradiction the analyse step finds against another question's standing `## Decisions` entry while recording an ordinary answer gets a note under `## Noted contradictions`, whether or not the answer plainly supersedes the old entry. The fold only appends the new decision, the old entry stays exactly as written, and the answer core's closing ban on otherwise rewriting `requirements.md` stays as it is for ordinary answers. An existing entry is rewritten only when a conflict question the review pass authored from the note is answered. Rewriting a decision recorded under another question always goes through one explicit, answerable conflict question, so no runner judgment of "plain supersession" ever silently changes an entry the user recorded earlier. The single-question fold keeps one rule with no judgment branch, and each answer commit's `requirements.md` diff stays exactly the folded decision plus at most a note. Every intended supersession, about 17 of the 38 pairs in the October 2 analysis, costs a review pass, a conflict question, its alternatives and recommendation, and another answer before the old entry is fixed, and the open conflict question blocks `/derive-tasks` in the meantime. It also forbids by rule what the Edit-based fold already does by runner judgment, as in the October 8 run that rewrote the superseded sentence during the fold.

The analyse step judges each contradiction it finds. When the new answer plainly supersedes the old entry, because the user's answer is clearly meant to replace it, the fold rewrites the conflicting text of that other question's entry in place in the same targeted edit pass, and writes no note. When the answer does not plainly settle which entry should hold, the old entry stays as written and a note is written. Doubt notes. The answer core's ban on otherwise rewriting `requirements.md` gains this one exception. The common case, an answer that knowingly replaces an earlier decision, is fixed in the same commit that records it, at no extra review, question, or answer cycle, and `requirements.md` never holds two contradicting sentences for that case. Only genuinely unsettled pairs reach the review pass, so noted contradictions stay rare and each one means a real open choice. One commit per answer still makes revert-then-re-answer restore the old entry. The supersession test is a runner judgment that can misfire, and a wrong rewrite silently edits a decision recorded under another question with nothing flagged. Only the commit diff shows it, and no question is held open for anyone to catch it. The rewritten lines also show up as added lines in that answer's `requirements.md` hunk, which `capture-milestone-principle-updates` reads as the recorded decision. Whether the recommendation skill makes the same judgment depends on which procedure carries the note step, which the note-writing-home sibling settles.

When the analyse step judges that the answer plainly supersedes another question's standing entry, the inline skill asks the user once in the conversation whether to rewrite that entry. It rewrites the entry in place on a yes and writes a note on a no or when there is no reply. When the answer does not plainly settle which entry should hold, it writes a note without asking. A supersession is fixed in the answer's own commit, with no review cycle, only when a human has confirmed it, so no runner judgment alone ever rewrites another question's decision. Every refused or unanswered rewrite still lands in the note path. It adds a confirmation prompt to the single-question answer skills, which the workflow otherwise avoids so that headless chains have no prompt nobody is there to answer. In a headless run it falls back to always noting, so the same answer gets different handling depending on how the skill was invoked. Each runner also needs its own wording for asking and for treating no reply.

open-question.question: What does the fold tool's replace mode replace: the whole body of the `###` subsection named by `--section` with the text on standard input, keeping the heading, or one entry inside that subsection identified by a further argument, given that a milestone's `## Decisions` holds either one prose paragraph per subsection or topical subsections of several `- **Lead.** text` bullets?

When the answer sweep's batched call records a conflict question whose answer rewrites entries under more than one `###` subsection, does that question's section carry one replace call per rewritten subsection chained ahead of its `remove`, or exactly one replace call for one subsection so every section keeps a fixed number of tool calls?
open-question.alternative: A conflict question's section carries one replace call for each `###` subsection the answer rewrites, as many as the decision needs, each its own `requirements.py` process on its own quoted heredoc, chained behind `&&` ahead of the section's `remove`. The rewrite scope is every entry the answer supersedes, including a clause correcting a third subsection that is not one of the two entries the question names. The section shape therefore varies: the shown call states the replace line as repeated once per rewritten subsection, and an ordinary question's section keeps its single fold. It is the only fixed-process-per-subsection shape that can fully remove superseded text wherever it sits. That covers the one recorded field case, where the sweep had to correct a clause living in a different subsection and could only append beside it, and it needs nothing from the tool beyond a single-subsection replace. The batched call loses its one fixed section shape: the runner composes a variable number of calls per conflict section, `tests/test_sweep_batched_call.py`'s extraction and the shown call need a repetition rule, and a refusal on the second replace leaves the first rewrite uncommitted for the stranded-fold guard to catch on the next run. How much one call rewrites depends on the replace mode's granularity, whole subsection body or one entry, which a sibling question owns.

A conflict question's section carries one replace call per subsection holding one of the two entries the question names, so one call when only the losing entry is rewritten or both sit under the same heading, and two when both named entries are rewritten under different headings. These are chained behind `&&` ahead of `remove`. Entries outside the named pair are never rewritten by the sweep, and any knock-on clause elsewhere is left standing for the next review pass's `## Decisions` consistency step. The count is bounded at two and follows from the question's own text, which names both headings, so the runner reads the call count off the question rather than judging how far the supersession reaches. That keeps the sweep close to its record-as-given stance while still allowing a reconciling answer that edits both entries. The section is still not one fixed shape (one or two replace calls), and the extraction test and shown call must show the optional second call. A supersession that reaches a third subsection survives the answer as a fresh conflict the next review pass has to re-author. Whether the winning entry is touched at all depends on how the conflict answer is recorded, which a sibling question owns.

Every conflict question's section carries exactly one replace call for exactly one subsection, the one holding the losing entry, chained ahead of `remove`. The sweep never rewrites a second subsection. The winning entry and any knock-on clause elsewhere stay as written, and a residual conflict is left to the next review pass's `## Decisions` consistency step to flag as a new question. Every section of the batched call thus keeps a fixed number of tool calls, with the conflict section differing from an ordinary one only in replace standing where fold stands. The batched call keeps one fixed section shape with no count for the runner to judge or the test to extract. That matches the sweep's measured failure mode, where variable composition is what produced ad-hoc scripts, and it keeps a refused replace an all-or-nothing stop for its question. An answer that genuinely supersedes text under two headings is recorded only in part: the second stale entry stays in `requirements.md` until another review-and-answer round, which is the appended-beside-the-old-text residue this milestone exists to remove. Whether the winning heading also gets a statement depends on the conflict answer record question, a sibling's.

A conflict question's section carries exactly one replace process that rewrites every subsection the answer supersedes in a single write. The replace mode takes the target headings and their new bodies together, for example a repeated `--section` with a delimited stdin, so the section's tool-call count stays fixed while the number of rewritten subsections varies. The tool resolves every named heading before it writes anything and refuses the whole replace, file unchanged, if any one fails. It keeps one fixed call per section and still lets a supersession reach every subsection it touches. One process makes the multi-subsection rewrite atomic, so no partial rewrite can be stranded, much as `remove` resolves every `--undermined` title before it changes anything. The fold tool gains a multi-target input format with its own delimiter, parsing, and tests, a larger surface than any other single-target tool call in the plugin. The runner still composes a variable-length heredoc whose structure must be right, so the composition risk moves into the stdin rather than disappearing. Its shape is conditioned on the replace mode's invocation and granularity, which sibling questions own.

Every conflict section the sweep writes carries exactly one replace call for the losing entry's subsection. A conflict question whose answer would rewrite more than one subsection gets no section in the batched call and is left standing for `answer-open-question-with-recommendation`, whose Edit-based fold can rewrite any number of entries by rule. The closing completeness `walk` then prints that id. The batched call keeps one fixed section shape, and the rare multi-subsection supersession is still recorded in full, on the path whose Edit-based fold already rewrites freely, so neither the tool nor the test grows for an edge case. It breaks the sweep's one-section-per-walked-question rule and its no-judgment stance: the runner must judge how far each conflict answer reaches before writing the call. The completeness `walk`'s print, now treated as an anomaly, would carry an expected id, so the report would need a new advisory naming the questions left for the single-question skill.

open-question.question: How does the answer sweep tell a conflict question, whose section uses the replace mode, from an ordinary one, given that a question block carries only its `id` and question text: by a fixed opening phrase the review pass writes into every conflict question's text, by a fixed Short Title convention such as a `Conflict:` prefix, or by the runner's own reading of the question text?

When a conflict question is answered and the losing entry is rewritten, is that rewrite the whole record of the decision, or is a decision statement also folded under the winning entry's heading, given that `capture-milestone-principle-updates` reads the recorded decision from the added lines of the answer commit's `requirements.md` hunk?

Does the review pass author one open question for every entry under `## Noted contradictions` exactly as noted, or apply its own conflict test to each note first and delete a note it judges to be a refinement rather than a conflict without authoring a block?
open-question.alternative: The review pass applies no test of its own to a note. Every entry under `## Noted contradictions` becomes exactly one block through step 3's `add`, its question built from the note's pair (the two `###` headings, what each entry says, which stands), and the note is then deleted. Not even a standing block that already flags the same pair, or a named entry that has since been rewritten, stops the authoring: the note is turned into a block exactly as written. The conflict judgment is made once, by the answer skill that saw the pair as it recorded the decision, and the review pass handles notes purely mechanically. A real conflict can never be lost to a second judgment that disagrees, and the review pass keeps its tidy-side role toward notes, with no reading of the note's merits. Every false positive and stale note costs a whole question cycle (alternatives, recommendation, answer) and holds `/derive-tasks`' precondition until that cycle is done. A pair that step 4's own scan already flagged, or one that a later answer has already settled, still produces a duplicate or moot block, which goes against the pass's existing dedup and prune rules. How self-standing the authored question can be depends on what a note entry holds, which the sibling question on note entry content decides.

alternative.id: Clean up against recorded state only

open-question.alternative: The review pass does not re-judge whether the pair conflicts. It checks each note only against what is already recorded. If a standing block already flags the pair, or if either named entry no longer stands as the note describes it (its heading is gone, or it has been rewritten so the two now hold together), the note is deleted with no block, as cleanup of recorded state. Every other note is authored as noted, one block per note, and then deleted. It applies to notes the same tidy-side rule the pass already uses for blocks: remove only what already-recorded state covers, an exact duplicate included. Duplicate and moot questions are avoided, while the answer skill's conflict verdict is never overruled on its merits. A note that was a refinement from the start, a false positive of the answer skill's analyse step, still becomes a question that holds task derivation for a full cycle. The check also needs the review pass to compare a note against the current entries, so its reliability depends on how precisely a note names its pair (the sibling question on note entry content) and on whether answers rewrite superseded entries in place (the sibling question on note versus rewrite at fold).

The review pass applies step 4's own conflict test to each note: both entries cannot hold as written, while an entry that only refines, narrows, or extends the other is no conflict. It also applies the recorded-state cleanup (the pair is already flagged, or an entry has since been rewritten). A note that passes becomes one block and is deleted. A note the pass judges plainly a refinement, or already covered, is deleted with no block. Doubt resolves toward authoring the block, so a note is dropped only when the refinement verdict is clear. Notes and step 4's own scan share one conflict test, so the set of conflict questions is the same whichever runner noticed the pair first. A false positive from an answer skill's analyse step costs nothing downstream: no alternatives, recommendation, or answer cycle, and no hold on `/derive-tasks`. The review pass now deletes a recorded conflict on its own judgment, with no block and no answer, which moves it past the tidy side's 'remove only what recorded state covers' line. A wrong refinement verdict loses a real conflict silently: only the `Requirements-review:` commit diff shows the deleted note, and the pair then reaches `/derive-tasks`, where only the tie-break rule settles it.

The review pass applies step 4's conflict test and the recorded-state cleanup to each note, as in the re-testing option. A note it confirms becomes one block and is deleted, and a note already covered by recorded state (pair already flagged, or an entry rewritten) is deleted with no block. A note it judges a refinement is neither authored nor deleted: it stays under `## Noted contradictions` and is named in the pass's report as a git-absent advisory, so the user can delete it by hand or have it authored. The next pass sees it again. It keeps the pass's 'when in doubt, flag rather than delete' rule. A note the pass disagrees with is never thrown away on the pass's judgment alone, yet it does not cost a question cycle or hold task derivation, because a kept note does not affect `list`'s convergence verdict. A third state appears, a note that is neither a question nor resolved. It can stay through convergence and task derivation, so `/derive-tasks`' tie-break and the handling of leftover notes at finish (the sibling question on leftover notes) must cover it. Every later pass re-tests it and repeats the advisory, and nothing in the workflow ever settles it unless the user acts.

open-question.question: How does `/derive-tasks` decide which of two conflicting `## Decisions` entries is the later-recorded one, given that a fold into an existing subsection lands earlier in the file than a newer subsection appended at the end: by position in the file, by the git history of the two entries, or by the note under `## Noted contradictions` naming which entry was recorded later?

Does the `/derive-tasks` tie-break rule apply only to the pairs listed under `## Noted contradictions`, or to any two `## Decisions` entries the runner finds cannot both hold while deriving the briefs?

When a milestone is finished with entries still standing under `## Noted contradictions`, because `/derive-tasks` was run without a further review pass, do those entries stay in the finished milestone's `requirements.md` untouched, or does `/finish-current-milestone` report them before it records the completion?
Is the fold tool's replace mode a flag on the existing `fold` subcommand, such as `fold --replace`, or a second subcommand of `requirements.py` with its own name?
open-question.alternative: Replace is an optional flag on the existing subcommand, `fold <MILESTONE_DIR> --section "<Heading>" --replace`, the new text on stdin. Without the flag the call appends exactly as it does today, so `fold`'s default, its current call shape, and every existing caller and test stay unchanged; with it the same subcommand takes the replace branch, and its help text and contract describe both behaviours. Smallest change to the tool and its callers: the sweep's batched call and `tests/test_sweep_batched_call.py` keep the one fold command they extract, and a conflict question's section differs from an ordinary one by a single token, which keeps the sweep's sections as close to one fixed shape as the milestone allows. One subcommand ends up with two behaviours: an append that never touches existing text and a replace that overwrites it. They may refuse different inputs, depending on what the missing-subsection sibling decides. A forgotten flag fails silently: the call appends instead of replacing, which is the field failure this milestone exists to remove (a correction paragraph added under the old heading while the original sentence still stands), and nothing in the call's exit status shows it.

Replace is a second subcommand of `requirements.py` with its own name, for example `replace <MILESTONE_DIR> --section "<Heading>"`, the new text on stdin. It has its own argparse parser, help text, and refusal set, and it reuses the file's internal readers, `## Decisions` locator, and atomic writer. `fold` stays exactly as it is, append-only, with its contract, call shape, and six test files untouched. Overwriting existing text gets a name of its own, separate from appending, in the same verb-per-operation style as the open-question tool's `lift`, `strip`, `embed`, and `remove`. Each subcommand keeps one behaviour and one refusal set, `fold`'s byte-preserving append-only contract stays true as stated in `CLAUDE.md` and the docs, and a call that names the wrong verb shows it in the command text itself. The tool's CLI grows a second entry point, with a second help text and its own contract and test files, and the stdin and `--section` handling is declared twice in the parser. The sweep's conflict-question section carries a different command from its ordinary sections, so the fence extraction in `tests/test_sweep_batched_call.py`, which finds the call by its fold command, has to handle or ignore a second command. How much that matters depends on the siblings that settle how conflict questions are recognised and how many replace calls a section carries.

`fold` takes a required, mutually exclusive mode group, `fold <MILESTONE_DIR> --section "<Heading>" (--append | --replace)`, with no default. A call that states neither mode fails with argparse's exit 2. The same pattern is used by the task-list tool's required position group and the open-question tool's `embed (--alternatives | --recommendation)`. The existing sweep call gains `--append`. No call can land in a mode it did not state: a call that forgot to replace stops with exit 2 instead of silently appending. That closes the silent-append failure the optional flag leaves open, and it follows the precedent the project already set for position and shape, where a missing choice must fail rather than default. It changes the contract of an existing, tested call for a mode that only conflict questions use. Every ordinary sweep section gains a token, the sweep's batched call, its extracting test, and every one of the six `test_requirements_*` files that invoke `fold` have to be updated, and one subcommand still holds both behaviours and both refusal sets.

open-question.question: When the fold tool's replace mode is given a `--section` heading that matches no `###` subsection under `## Decisions`, does it refuse with one `Error:` line and leave the file unchanged, or create the subsection at the end of the section as `fold` does?
open-question.alternative: The replace mode matches `--section` against the `###` headings under `## Decisions` with the same whitespace- and case-folded exact equality `fold` uses. When no subsection matches, it prints one `Error:` line on stderr naming the heading, exits 1, and leaves `requirements.md` byte-for-byte unchanged. It never creates a subsection, so a replace can only rewrite an entry that already exists. `fold` keeps its create-at-end behaviour. A replace exists to rewrite an entry that is already standing, so a heading matching nothing is always a mistake: a mistyped heading, or the runner pointing at the wrong pair. Refusing turns that mistake into a visible stop. The sweep's batched call already treats a fold refusal as a resumable `stopped at` with the tree left as it was. Creating instead would leave the superseded entry standing beside a new subsection, which is the both-entries-standing outcome this milestone sets out to remove. The reason `fold` creates a missing heading (so one call shape can serve a fresh milestone's first decision) has no counterpart here, because there is never a first entry to replace. Every refusal stops the sweep's batched call. A near-miss heading that a human would read as the intended subsection halts the whole run at that question until someone corrects the heading and re-runs. The tool's two writing modes also handle the same input differently, which adds one refusal case to the tests and one more case for the runtime prose to keep apart from `fold`'s create rule.

When `--section` matches no `###` subsection, the replace mode behaves exactly as `fold` does on a missing heading. It creates the subsection at the end of `## Decisions` and writes the stdin body under it. Nothing is refused and nothing existing is rewritten. On an unmatched heading, a replace is indistinguishable from a fold, and the writes are a success. The two modes share one rule for an unmatched heading, so the tool has no new refusal case and the sweep's conflict-question section can never stop on a heading. The batched call keeps the property that a well-formed decision always lands, and any near-duplicate subsection the creation produces shows in that answer's commit diff and stays revertable. A wrong or mistyped heading fails silently. The losing entry stays standing unchanged and the new text lands under a fresh subsection, so the conflict the question was meant to settle is recorded as two standing entries again, with no stop and no `Error:` line. The milestone's goal is to rewrite superseded entries instead of appending beside them, and this outcome is exactly what that goal targets. The only remaining catch is a later review pass's consistency step noticing the pair again.

The replace mode takes an optional flag (named, for example, `--create`). Without the flag, an unmatched heading is refused with one `Error:` line and the file left unchanged. With the flag, an unmatched heading creates the subsection at the end of `## Decisions` as `fold` does. Each call decides, so the caller chooses per invocation whether a missing subsection is an error or a place to write. Both behaviours are available. The default guards against a mistyped heading silently leaving a superseded entry standing, and a caller that knows the heading is new can still write the rewrite without switching to `fold`. Only the sweep calls the tool, and its batched call has one fixed section shape with no branch per question kind. Using the flag on some questions and not others would bring in exactly the per-question judgment and call variation the fixed shape exists to rule out. Always passing it, or never passing it, collapses this option into one of the other two while still paying for an extra flag, its tests, and its one-sentence contract at the call site. If replace is a flag on `fold` rather than its own subcommand (the invocation question decides this), a second modifier flag on the same subcommand also complicates the argparse contract.
